body.heading: Sixty seconds is enough
paragraphs: Hold the door and actually wait, instead of letting it swing. Text the friend who went quiet last week. Leave the last slice for someone else. None of these take more than a minute, and none of them will be noticed by the wider world. They still count.

The trick is that one-minute kindness is mostly about noticing. The person behind you in line has their hands full. A coworker is carrying something heavy in more ways than one. Attention is the real gift; the act itself is usually small.

body.heading: A few to try today
paragraphs: Say thank you like you mean it, with the reason attached: thanks for staying late, thanks for the ride, thanks for remembering. Specific thanks land differently than a general one.

Offer the thing you can actually give. A spare umbrella, a phone charger, the good seat by the window. Small, concrete offers are easier to accept than grand gestures, and much easier to make a habit of.

description: Most kindness does not need money, planning, or a free afternoon — it needs sixty seconds and a little attention.
